title: DIRECTIVE, METACOGNITIVE OR A BLEND OF BOTH? A COMPARISON OF AI-GENERATED FEEDBACK TYPES ON STUDENT ENGAGEMENT, CONFIDENCE, AND OUTCOMES
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether different types of generative AI feedback produce different effects on learners’ engagement, confidence, and quality of work. The authors focus on a longstanding feedback-design question: whether directive feedback, which gives explicit corrections and suggestions, or metacognitive feedback, which prompts reflection and self-regulation, is more effective. They also test a hybrid approach that combines both. The study is framed as addressing a gap in direct comparative evidence using consistent AI-generated feedback delivered at scale.

The intervention was implemented through the RiPPLE adaptive educational platform in a semester-long randomized controlled trial. Students were randomly assigned to receive one of three AI-generated feedback types on resources they created for a design and programming course: directive, metacognitive, or hybrid. All feedback shared the same summary and strengths sections, while only the suggestions-for-improvement section differed by condition. Outcomes included linguistic differences in generated feedback, engagement time, whether students revised after feedback, confidence ratings, and final resource quality.

The population consisted of 329 students in an introductory university design and programming course at the University of Queensland. Most participants were undergraduates, with smaller numbers of postgraduate and non-award students; many were international students and a majority studied English as a second language. The intervention occurred over a 12-week semester via an online platform used for course-related collaborative learning tasks, including creation, moderation, and practice with peer-generated resources.

The main conclusion is that AI feedback type influenced revision behavior but not confidence, time-on-task, or final work quality. Hybrid feedback prompted the highest revision rates, directive feedback also outperformed metacognitive feedback on revision, and metacognitive feedback led to the lowest likelihood of revision. However, confidence remained similarly high across groups and resource quality outcomes were statistically comparable. The authors argue that hybrid AI feedback may be the most promising design because it combines actionable guidance with reflective prompting, though the study was conducted in a single higher-education course with relatively high baseline performance and no long-term follow-up beyond the course.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled trial with a sizable sample and clear analytic methods, which supports relatively strong internal validity. However, it is a higher-education preprint rather than K-12 evidence, uses proximal course-specific outcomes rather than standardized achievement measures, and therefore has some relevance and credibility concerns for the requested K-12 literacy evidence base.
impact_tier_rationale: The study found no significant impact on academic performance outcomes and mixed effects on engagement-related process measures, with benefits limited to revision behavior rather than end outcomes. Because there is no demonstrated positive effect on learning outcomes and the population is not K-12, overall impact is best classified as red.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated feedback on student-created course resources in an adaptive platform, experimentally varying directive, metacognitive, and hybrid feedback styles to influence revision behavior, confidence, and work quality.
RiPPLE adaptive platform used as the delivery environment for resource creation, peer evaluation, adaptive practice, and AI feedback within a university design/programming course.

finding.finding_summary: In a semester-long randomized controlled trial with 329 higher-education students, AI feedback type significantly affected one engagement indicator—revision behavior—but not time-on-task or confidence. Students in the hybrid condition revised most often (27.5%), followed by directive (21.1%) and metacognitive (12.1%); directive feedback produced higher odds of revision than metacognitive feedback (OR=2.93, 95% CI [1.25, 6.88], p=.009), and hybrid feedback also exceeded metacognitive feedback (equivalently about 4.3x higher odds; 95% CI [1.82, 10.0], p<.001), while engagement time and confidence showed no significant group differences (engagement: chi-square(2)=4.48, p=.107; confidence: chi-square=0.96, p=.62).
finding.measure: Behavioral engagement via revision/action on feedback, engagement time in seconds, and self-reported confidence ratings on a 1-5 scale
finding.effect_size: OR=2.93 for Directive vs Metacognitive; Hybrid vs Metacognitive approximately OR=4.3; otherwise not_reported
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI [1.25, 6.88] for Directive vs Metacognitive; 95% CI [1.82, 10.0] for Hybrid vs Metacognitive

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively targets metacognitive engagement and self-regulated learning through reflective versus directive AI feedback, but the measured evidence is indirect. Hybrid and directive feedback led to more revision behavior than metacognitive feedback, suggesting greater uptake of feedback, yet the study found no significant differences in confidence or final resource quality, and it did not directly measure validated self-regulation or metacognitive skill growth.
finding.measure: Indirect indicators of self-regulated learning and metacognitive engagement, including revision behavior, task-flow transitions, and confidence ratings
finding.effect_size: OR=2.93 for Directive vs Metacognitive revision odds; Hybrid vs Metacognitive approximately OR=4.3; otherwise not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Across 329 students, AI-generated feedback type did not significantly change final resource quality in a design/programming course. Back-transformed estimated means were 3.62 for directive, 3.72 for metacognitive, and 3.75 for hybrid feedback on a 1-5 resource-quality scale, with no significant overall group effect (chi-square=1.40, p=.49).
finding.measure: Resource quality scores (1-5) based on platform evaluation combining peer ratings, instructor moderation, and algorithmic adjustments
finding.confidence_interval: Directive 95% CI [3.45, 3.78]; Metacognitive 95% CI [3.55, 3.87]; Hybrid 95% CI [3.59, 3.91]
